It decides *where and how* an agent runs, not *what* it does; it therefore [implements](../sdlc-stage/index.md) no SDLC stage and connects to the ontology only through the [[#Patterns enabled|patterns]] it provides as substrate. ```mermaid flowchart LR E["engineer
uv run adws/adw_*.py '…'"] --> V["validate roster
agents.validate()
before anything spawns"] V --> P["phase
with run.phase(PhaseParams)"] P --> A["kind=agent
ph.call(AgentCall)
spawn / resume pi"] P --> C["kind=code
quality.py · git · changes
no model, no tokens"] A --> J["parse envelope
against output_type"] J -->|no| CORR["correct in the
same session"] CORR --> J J -->|yes| G["gates
verify the claims"] G -->|violations| CORR G -->|green| PERM["permissions sweep
diff repo before/after;
roll back stray writes"] C --> ENV["as_envelope()
code result, same door"] ENV --> P PERM --> P P --> F["run.finish(accepted=…)
exit code · session status · banner"] A -.->|every event, live| DB[("sssf.db
WAL SQLite")] C -.-> DB G -.-> DB ``` **Super Simple Software Factory** (IndyDevDan, `disler/super-simple-software-factory`, MIT) is a **deterministic Python control plane for coding agents, delivered as a Claude Code skill you stamp into a repo**. Its thesis fits on one line — *"Deterministic Python owns the graph. Coding agents are bounded nodes inside it"* — and its slogan is **"Agent proposes, code disposes."** An **ADW** (AI Developer Workflow) script owns sequencing, retries, and acceptance; agents work inside named *phases*; typed JSON envelopes carry context across the seams; every event streams into SQLite while it is still happening. It sits at the **library pole** of the runtime layer alongside [[sandcastle]] — you write the coordination yourself — but where Sandcastle is an SDK you import, sssf is a **template you stamp and then edit**, which is a different distribution shape for the same pole. ## Why this is a runtime and not a framework It is the closest call in this namespace so far, and worth recording because the ingest checklist's [step 0](../CONVENTIONS.md#ingest-workflow-reminders) says a misfiled node drags everything with it. Three things point *toward* framework: it ships a five-agent roster (planner · builder · scout · reviewer · documenter), a set of prompts, and twelve starter chains, one of which (`adw_simple_sdlc`) walks plan → build → test → review → document. That is a lifecycle. The classification still lands on `runtime`, on three tests: - **It hosts no agent loop and spawns the one that does.** `agent_pi.py` builds the argv, launches [[pi]] as a subprocess, tails its JSONL stdout, and reaps it. That is the runtime-versus-harness test, cleanly. - **The process content is explicitly disposable and the control plane is not.** The README is unusually direct about this: *"The tests it ships are not your tests. The prompts it ships describe a demo app, not your domain. The roster names the models that were good the week it was written. All of that is supposed to be replaced."* What you keep is `adw_modules/` — phases, envelopes, gates, permissions, tracing, session resumption. A framework's methodology is the product; here the methodology is sample data and the *substrate* is the product. - **The pitch is a relocation of the control plane, not a method.** *"This fixes that by moving the control plane out of the prompt and into Python."* The thing being moved is sequencing, retries, and acceptance — the execution layer's own concerns, taken back from the model. The tell the conventions name — *"a page whose capabilities almost all map to no stage is rarely a framework"* — cuts the same way from the other side: the stamped surface is `run.phase()`, `ph.call()`, `gates.*`, `quality.*`, `permissions.*`. None of those perform a lifecycle step. The role prompts do, and they are the part you are told to throw away. ## The distinguishing claim: the control plane leaves the prompt Every runtime here argues something about where coordination belongs. [[bernstein]] argues it belongs in a scheduler with no model in it; sssf argues something narrower and more portable — that **the seams belong in code**, and that the reason a run is not repeatable is that it has none: > Hand a capable model your whole SDLC and you get a machine with no seams. There is no phase boundary, so you cannot say which step failed. There is no acceptance criterion you can name, so "done" means "the agent stopped talking." A retry is a cold start that throws away everything the agent just learned. The only trace is a transcript you have to read like a novel. Run it twice, get two different systems. Four consequences are drawn from that one decision, and each is a mechanism below: phases become the unit of the trace; envelopes become the only way context crosses a seam; gates become the definition of done; and a correction becomes cheaper than a restart because the session is still alive. *"Same models. Same prompts. The difference is who owns the loop."* The second, sharper claim is about **when not to use an agent at all**, and it is the one the wiki has least of elsewhere: > Code costs nothing. It runs at the speed of light. You can change it in a second. And you actually own it, which is not true of any model you are renting by the token. So when the invocation is already known, write it down. `bun test` is not a judgement call. Neither is `ruff check`. An agent rediscovering your test runner burns a context window to learn what a subprocess already knows […] Worse, it puts a passing test suite into a context window, which buys you nothing at all. This is a hard rule of the skill, not an aside (*"A known command is code, not an agent"*), and it is why the shipped roster has **no tester agent**. It is also, in a different vocabulary, [[topic-harness-engineering]]'s rule that a computational control beats an inferential one wherever a computational one exists — arrived at here from cost and repeatability rather than from control theory. ## The phase primitive: three lanes, one context manager Every run is a sequence of phases and every phase is the same `with run.phase(PhaseParams(...))` block, whoever owns it. Three `kind`s, three swim lanes in the trace: - **`engineer`** — the human lane; today the phase that records who asked and for what. - **`agent`** — `ph.call(AgentCall(...))`: prompt in, typed envelope out, gates verified. - **`code`** — a deterministic step that stands on its own (a commit, the suite, a diff capture), **never buried inside an agent phase**, so the trace shows exactly when code ran and when an agent was working. Two rules give the primitive its teeth. **Success must be earned**: a phase is constructed `status="fail"` and only a clean exit flips it, with an agent phase additionally needing its envelope to parse and every gate green. And **the run's outcome is a second question, asked separately** — `run.finish(accepted=...)` exists because *"a test phase that ran a red suite did its job perfectly"*; the phase succeeded and the run must not. The docstring records that this replaced a `succeeded` property whose side effects wrote the session green in the database, the terminal, and the UI while the process exited 1: *"Anyone reading the trace saw success; only a CI job checking `$?` saw the truth."* One call now settles the exit code, the session status, and the banner together *"so the three cannot disagree"* — a small thing, and the clearest example in this layer of a trace being treated as a load-bearing artifact rather than a log. Every phase must also carry a `description` — one sentence of intent, rejected at construction if blank or a restatement of the name (`commit_plan: "Commit the plan"` is refused), because it is the only intent the trace, the console, and the UI ever show. ## Envelopes: the contract at every seam An agent has **exactly two output channels** and no others: reference files written into the session's shared `context_handoff/`, and a final valid-JSON response parsed against the `output_type` the call declared. Code persists that response as `envelope.json`, records it, and injects it into the next agent's user prompt via `{{previous_envelope}}`. **Context transfers in code, not in conversation.** ```python class EnvelopeBase(BaseModel): status: Literal["success", "fail"] summary: str = "" artifacts: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list) notes_for_next_agent: str = "" ``` Subtypes add what their consumer needs — `BuildOutput.changed_files` and `commit_message` (read by the git phase), `ReviewOutput.approved`/`findings`/`blocking`, `ScoutOutput.findings`, `DocumentOutput.document_path`. Three properties are worth lifting out: - **The envelope is a manifest of claims**, which is what makes the gates below checkable at all. - **Deterministic results wear the same shape.** `quality.as_envelope(result)` and `changes.as_envelope(changeset)` adapt a test run and a `git diff` into envelopes, so a code phase hands its result to the next agent *through the same door* an agent's report would have used — *"the consuming agent cannot tell the difference, which is the point."* One repair loop serves both. - **The contract is a synced triad** — the Pydantic type in `data_types.py`, the JSON example in that agent's `user.md` `## Report` section, and `output_type=` at the call site are *one thing*, and the skill's hard rules require all three to change in the same edit. Drift between them is paid for on every call in correction rounds. ## Gates: verify the claims, never the predictions A gate is `gate(envelope, run) -> GateReport`, and gates run **after** the agent finishes, against what it declared: *"Nobody knows which files an agent will touch before it finishes."* The shipped set is small and entirely mechanical — `artifacts_exist`, `files_non_empty`, `json_parses`, `diff_matches_claims`, `verdict_consistent`, and a `tests_pass(command)` factory. Each returns one `check(item, ok, note)` per thing it looked at, so a *green* gate can answer **what did you verify** (`{"item": "…/plan.md", "ok": true, "note": "exists, 454B"}`) rather than only *did it pass* — evidence, not a verdict, landing in both `gate_results` and the event stream. `verdict_consistent` is the sharpest of them and the one worth stealing: it checks a review envelope **against itself** — an approval that ships blocking items, or a rejection that names no problem, *"is a claim the harness can refute without reading a line of the diff."* Judging the code is still the reviewer's job; judging the reviewer's internal consistency is free. The skill is candid about the ceiling: *"Gates check what a predicate can check, not plan quality or code taste. Run the reviewer, or read it yourself."* ## Correction, not restart When JSON fails to parse or a gate returns violations, **nothing restarts**. The harness re-prompts the *same* agent session with a correction naming exactly what was wrong; the context window stays intact. Parse failures are bounded by `JSON_FIX_ATTEMPTS` (2), gate violations by the phase's own `retries`. Pi treats `--session-id` as create-or-continue, so *running* an agent and *continuing* it are the same call — the runtime never needs a separate resume path. *"A cold restart throws away everything the agent learned. A correction costs one message."* The same mechanism scales up to whole workflows. `agent_map.json` records agent → session id → model per `adw_id`, so `adw_build.py --adw-id a1b2c3d4` run after `adw_plan.py` rejoins the builder's **existing context window** rather than starting cold. The map stores the model each session was created with and starts a fresh session if config drift changed it — *"never a bad resume."* ## Permissions: `tools` is a capability list, `writes` is the boundary The cleanest piece of engineering in the repo, and the reason this runtime supplies [[pattern-edit-guardrails]]. The argument first: a tool allowlist cannot express a safety boundary, because two of the tools are general-purpose — `bash` runs anything including `git checkout`, and `write` reaches any path. *"So 'this agent changes nothing' is a claim a tool list can state but never keep."* `permissions.py` keeps it the same way every other claim in the system is kept — **after the fact, against the repo**. The working tree's change-set is fingerprinted before the agent's first prompt and again after its last send (retries and gate corrections included); any path that appeared, vanished, or changed is attributed to that agent. Comparing change-sets rather than watching writes is deliberate: *"a path that was modified before the agent ran and is clean afterwards has been **reverted**, and a reversion is a modification. That is what catches `git checkout`."* A breach is explicitly **not** a gate violation — *"Gates are for work an agent can be asked to redo; a write has already happened, so re-prompting fixes nothing."* Instead every unauthorized change the agent *introduced* is rolled back (tracked files with `git checkout --`, untracked by deletion), a path that was **already dirty** beforehand is left alone (*"the operator had uncommitted work there, and discarding it to tidy up would be the same harm this module exists to prevent"*), and the phase fails naming every path and what happened to it. Two config keys drive it. Per-agent `writes:` declares what that agent may change in the repo (`[]` = nothing; omitted = unrestricted); roster-wide `protected_files:` fences `adws/adw_modules/`, `adws/adw_sssf_config/`, and `adws/adw_*.py` from everyone — **an agent must not be able to edit the machinery that grades it**. The session runtime under `data_dir` is always writable for everyone, and the reasoning is exact: a read-only agent must be *"read-only with respect to the REPO, never mute"*, and that grant comes from `data_dir` rather than from `.gitignore` because an agent's ability to record its own work *"must not depend on a gitignore line someone can delete."* ## The roster: one model per phase `sssf.config.yaml` answers one question per entry — *who is this agent* — and the ADW call site answers the other — *how is it used*. **ADW scripts name agents, never models**, which is what lets one agent serve many calls. Each entry sets the core four (context, model, prompt, tools) plus `thinking` (pi's `off … max` ladder), a `color` for its lane in the trace, `harness_engineering` pi extensions, and its `writes` boundary. The starter roster **deliberately mixes vendors** to make the point that model choice is per-phase: `kimi-k3` on Fireworks for the planner at `thinking: high`, Gemini Flash for the builder and scout, two different OpenAI models for the reviewer and documenter. *"It is not about which model is best anymore, it is about which model is right for that one phase."* The side effect is that the shipped reviewer runs a **different vendor's model than the builder** — but that is a property of one roster, not an enforced precondition, so this page does not claim [[pattern-cross-model-review]]; [[bernstein]]'s review gate, which raises `DifferentModelRequired` when it cannot get one, is what enforcement of that pattern looks like. Validation is front-loaded: every ADW declares `REQUIRED_AGENTS` and calls `agents.validate()` before anything spawns, checking that each named agent exists, resolves to a usable coding agent and model, and has both prompt files on disk. **No agent is ever spawned against a half-valid config.** The one honest gap is named in the README: `validate()` checks that a model is *written* as `provider/model-id`, not that its key is set, so a missing credential *"fails when that agent runs, partway into a chain."* ## Observability: one data path *"Agents write to SQLite, readers poll SQLite."* `agent_pi.py` tails pi's JSONL stdout line by line and the tracer inserts each event **while the agent is still working**, so tool calls are visible mid-run instead of batched at the end. Ten event types (`phase_start`, `agent_start`, `tool_call`, `handoff`, `gate_pass`/`gate_fail`, `log`, `agent_end`, `phase_end`, `error`) land across seven tables — `sessions`, `phases`, `events`, `envelopes`, `gate_results`, `agent_sessions`, `processes` — each logged against both its `adw_id` and its `phase_id`, with `parent_id` nesting spans so an agent phase expands into its own tool calls. ```sql select * from events where adw_id = ? and rowid > ? order by rowid limit 500; ``` That single rowid-cursor query **is the entire transport**: live view and full history are the same query at different cadence, *"which is why there is no ingest endpoint, no WebSocket, no backfill, and no separate replay path."* Every connection opens WAL, so reads never block a running writer. Files stay the raw record (`raw_output.jsonl`, `envelope.json`, `agent_map.json`) and the database is the queryable mirror — *"losing it loses nothing you cannot rebuild."* A read-only Vue/Vite visualizer (Bun, port 4600) polls it, resolving its target through `--db` → `SSSF_DB` → `/adws/adw_data/sssf.db` so one instance can point at any stamped repo. Three details show the layer taking its own telemetry seriously. **Spend is itemised per phase** across `input`/`output`/`cache_read`/`cache_write` and summed over *every* send a phase made, so a phase that burned two correction rounds shows what all of them cost. **Context is occupancy, not spend** — `context_tokens` measures how full the window was when the agent stopped, computed exactly the way pi computes it for its own footer and auto-compaction trigger, so the number matches the harness's. And the `processes` table exists for the one failure the trace cannot otherwise show: *"A hung agent emits nothing, which is exactly when you need its pid."* `just procs` lists what is live, `just kill` stops children before the parent and verifies the recorded command still matches the pid, and a killed run finalizes its own trace — SIGTERM and SIGINT become `SystemExit` so the session lands on `fail` instead of reading `running` forever. ## The twelve starter workflows Every ADW takes the same shape — `uv run adws/adw_*.py "" [--config …] [--adw-id …]` — and is 40 to 180 lines on purpose, so copying the closest one and editing the phase list is the intended way to get a new chain. | ADW | Chain | Reach for it when | |---|---|---| | `adw_prompt` | engineer → \ | one agent, one prompt; `--agent NAME` picks who | | `adw_scout` | engineer → scout | read-only recon, nothing changes | | `adw_plan` | engineer → planner | you want the spec before any code | | `adw_build` | engineer → builder | the plan already exists | | `adw_quality` | engineer → code(quality) | lint, typecheck, build — no agents at all | | `adw_plan_build` | planner → builder → git(commit) | small, well-understood work | | `adw_build_test` | builder → code(test) → bounded fix loop | there is a suite to satisfy | | `adw_build_review` | builder → reviewer → bounded revise loop | *"is this what was asked for"* matters more than *"does it run"* | | `adw_plan_build_test` | plan → build → code(test) → git(commit) | the standard chain | | `adw_plan_build_test_quality` | same, plus lint/typecheck/build gates | the repo has quality commands worth enforcing | | `adw_document` | code(git diff) → documenter | write up what just shipped | | `adw_simple_sdlc` | plan → build → test → review → document, three commits | the work is real and its shape is not obvious | `adw_simple_sdlc` is the one to read: it asks the two questions separately and in order (*"The suite asks 'does it run'; the reviewer asks 'is this what was asked for' […] neither can answer the other's"*), re-runs the suite when a review revision changed code after the last green result, commits the code **only** once both came back clean, and lands three commits from three authors — the plan, the code, and the write-up each in the words of the agent that produced it, because *"reusing one agent's sentence for another's diff is how a commit log starts lying."* A failed run therefore leaves the plan committed and the working tree dirty, deliberately. ## Delivered as a skill, operated by a second harness The runtime layer's first instance whose install *and* operating surface is a harness skill. `.claude/skills/sssf/` is the whole product: `SKILL.md` holds the hard rules and a request-routing table, nine cookbooks are lazy-loaded one per request, `references/` holds the deep specs, `scripts/install.py` stamps `templates/` into the target repo (idempotent — a re-run skips what exists and doubles as a drift check; `--force` overwrites everything including your config and prompts). That produces a **two-harness topology unique in this layer**: [[claude-code]] loads the skill and plays *orchestrator* — launching ADWs, reading the trace database, editing the roster — while [[pi]] is the harness the runtime actually spawns to do the work. Only the second is a `runs:` edge; Claude Code is upstream of the runtime, not spawned by it. The skill polices the split with unusually explicit rules: *"You run the system, observe the system, and help the user interact with it. You do no ADW work yourself"* — never implement, plan, or test in an agent's place; never edit files under `sessions/`; query the trace database *"when observing is the task"*, never to volunteer a status report nobody asked for. The startup discipline is itself a [[pattern-context-engineering]] argument worth recording, because it is stated as a debugged failure rather than a preference: read the overview, list the ADWs, **stop**. No trace queries, no repo inventory, no "current state" dashboard — *"Volunteered state is guessed state. An orchestrator that improvised a status board queried a `runs` table and a `payload` column — neither exists"*, and the spec that would have said so was one lazy read away. Plus: *"It is stale on arrival. State printed before the request describes a system that the very next run changes."* ## What it deliberately does not do Unusually for this layer, the omissions are enumerated by the author rather than discovered by the reader, and they define the page's honest edges: - **No isolation of any kind.** *"It runs on your current branch. There is no sandbox, no branch per run, no merge step, no cloud, and no human-in-the-loop approval phase."* This is the only runtime here that supplies **none** of [[pattern-worktree-isolation]] — the guarantee it offers instead is the post-hoc permissions rollback above, which is a boundary on *what* was changed, not on *where*. - **No parallelism.** A chain is a sequence of phases in one process. No fan-out, no DAG, no [[pattern-wave-parallelism]]. - **No branch → PR.** Commits land on the current branch; there is no PR path. - **No memory across runs.** Nothing accumulates between `adw_id`s — no lessons, no diaries, no store. Contrast [[warren]]'s `.mulch/` and [[bernstein]]'s confidence-decayed lessons. - **Pi only, in v1.** `coding_agent: claude_code` is schema-valid and `agent_cc.py` raises `NotImplementedError`; the interface is specced (`claude -p --output-format stream-json --resume`) and deferred to v2. - **The shipped quality blocks are placeholders that exit 0**, announced loudly in a box comment and in the README's failure table, on the reasoning that *"a wrong-but-plausible command that silently passes is worse than one that says so out loud."* Until they are replaced, three of the twelve ADWs have a test phase that is theater. It is named as the first thing to customize. The scope answer is equally direct: *"Is this overkill for a one-off feature? Yes. Prompt an agent and move on. This earns its keep when the same workflow runs a hundred times, when validation is the only thing standing between you and a bad merge, and when you need the thousandth run to look like the first."* ## Orchestration profile | Concern | sssf | |---|---| | Isolation | **none** — runs on the current branch in the current tree; the substitute is a post-hoc permissions sweep that rolls back unauthorized writes | | Parallelism | **none** — one process, one sequence of phases | | Coordination logic | your Python — a 40–180-line ADW script composing `run.phase()` blocks; no DSL, no model in the loop | | Autonomy / AFK | a chain runs unattended to a two-part terminal gate (all phases green **and** `accepted=`), with bounded fix/revise loops; no cron, no long-lived daemon | | Verification | **gates over the envelope's claims** (`artifacts_exist`, `diff_matches_claims`, `verdict_consistent`, `tests_pass(cmd)`) + `kind="code"` quality blocks; violations return to the same session as corrections | | Steering (HITL) | none mid-run — the human lane is the `engineer` phase at the top and the exit code at the bottom | | Persistence / memory | per-session only — `agent_map.json` resumes an agent's own context window across ADWs; nothing compounds between sessions | | Provider-agnostic | **harness**: pi only in v1 (claude_code stubbed). **Model**: fully agnostic and per-phase — any `provider/model-id` in pi's catalog, a different one per agent in the same run | | Branch → PR | — | | Governance / audit | the trace *is* the audit: 7 tables, 10 event types, per-phase itemised spend, gate evidence, pid table; plus `writes`/`protected_files` enforcement | | Topology | a stamped `adws/` directory in the target repo; `uv run` per workflow; optional Bun visualizer reading the SQLite file | | Distribution | **library** — but stamped from a Claude Code **skill** rather than imported as a package; # Pattern: Tooling leverage (build the lever, not the result)

For any non-trivial work — bulk edits, a migration, an analysis, a check — **build the tool that does it or proves it instead of doing it by hand**. A codemod, a script, a generator, or a skill the subagents follow. The result is then a by-product of something re-runnable.

The second clause is the load-bearing one and is what separates this from ordinary automation advice: ***the tool is the artifact a reviewer can rerun***. The point is not that the agent works faster. It is that a reviewer who does not trust the agent's claim can re-derive the result themselves, which converts an assertion into evidence. That makes this the constructive complement of [[pattern-evidence-before-claims]]: one says a claim needs proof, this one says **build the thing that produces the proof**.

It also answers a failure mode specific to agents. An agent that edits 200 call sites by hand produces 200 opportunities to silently diverge and no way to check; an agent that writes the codemod produces one artifact whose correctness is inspectable and whose application is uniform. [[pstack]] states it as a principle explicitly scoped *to any non-trivial work, not just bulk work*, closing the loophole where "this is only a few files" defeats it.

## Applied by (backlinks)

pstack:

- [[pstack-principle-build-the-lever]] — the principle statement, with the reviewer-rerun clause.
- [[pstack-create-verification-skill]] — generates a per-repository harness that drives the real app, so behavior can be proven rather than asserted.
- [[pstack-blast-radius]] — rung 4 of its evidence ladder is a script that calls the real code and fails loud, shipped in the writeup.
- [[pstack-show-me-your-work]] — prefers evidence produced by committed scripts over hand-made one-offs.

## See Also

- [[pattern-deterministic-gates]] — what the lever often becomes once the lesson is worth enforcing.
- [[pattern-knowledge-compounding]] — a lever kept and reused is how tooling compounds.
EOF

# Pattern: Idempotent operations

Design commands, lifecycle steps, and processing loops to **converge to the same end state regardless of partial prior runs**. Re-running is always safe; a crash, a restart, or a retry mid-way leaves no half-state the next run has to reason about.

This is classic operational engineering, but it acquires a specific edge in agent work, which is why it earns a pattern page here rather than staying an implementation detail. Agent runs are **interrupted far more often than human ones** — context compaction, a session ending, a killed subagent, a cloud worker dropping out, an operator pressing stop. Every long-horizon capability in this wiki therefore depends on its steps being re-enterable, and the frameworks that run unattended lean on it hardest. It is the precondition that makes [[pattern-autonomous-loop]] and [[pattern-session-handoff]] safe: a resumed session can re-run the last step rather than having to determine exactly how far the dead one got.

Its most visible expression is a setup or configuration command that **overwrites its whole output** rather than patching it, so a second run cannot accumulate drift from the first.

## Applied by (backlinks)

pstack:

- [[pstack-principle-make-operations-idempotent]] — the principle statement, scoped to commands, lifecycle steps, and loops that run amid crashes and retries.
- [[pstack-setup-pstack]] — overwrites the whole model-role rule file on every run so re-runs stay idempotent.
- [[pstack-benny-setup]] — a re-runnable install that preserves destination-only files and reviews conflicts instead of overwriting local edits.

## See Also

- [[pattern-session-handoff]] — resumption is cheap when re-running a step is free.
- [[pattern-deterministic-gates]] — both make a run's outcome independent of how it got there.
EOF

# Pattern: Candidate grafting (bakeoff, then harvest the losers)

Run N independent attempts at the **same** artifact, pick the strongest as a base, then **walk each losing candidate for the one or two ideas worth porting into the base** before verifying the result. The losers are a parts bin, not waste.

The graft step is what distinguishes this from the two neighbouring patterns it is easily confused with. [[pattern-throwaway-prototype]] builds competing sketches to *make a decision* and then discards them — [[gstack-design-shotgun]]'s mockup variants and [[mp-prototype]]'s throwaway sketches both end that way. [[pattern-cross-model-review]] runs several models over *one* artifact to find its flaws. Candidate grafting has several models each produce a *whole* artifact and then treats the non-winners as a source of material. The claim is that a losing design is rarely uniformly worse; it usually solved one sub-problem better, and that part is recoverable at near-zero cost once the work already exists.

Three supporting mechanisms travel with it in the evidence:

- **The rubric is derived before fan-out and withheld from the candidates.** They see only the task; the rubric is the picker's tool afterwards. That keeps candidates from optimizing for the score instead of the problem.
- **Each candidate returns a rationale naming what it considered and rejected**, which is what makes the graft pass cheap — the alternatives are already articulated.
- **A cross-judge on a different model family scores independently**, and a disagreement between judge and parent is read as evidence that *the rubric was ambiguous*, not merely that one reader was wrong.

Isolation is a precondition: each candidate writes to its own worktree or output path, per [[pattern-worktree-isolation]], or the attempts contaminate each other.

## Applied by (backlinks)

- [[pstack-arena]] — the pattern's full six-phase realization (frame, fan out, cross-judge, pick, graft, verify).
- [[pstack-architect]] — Phase B runs an arena over design sketches and requires two structurally distinct candidates before synthesis.
- [[pstack-principle-exhaust-the-design-space]] — the principle that mandates competing candidates before committing.
- [[pstack-blast-radius]] — escalates to an arena for a big or wide change, merging what different models each caught.

- [[pattern-wave-parallelism]] — the fan-out mechanics; grafting is what happens after the wave returns.
- [[pattern-worktree-isolation]] — the precondition that keeps candidates independent.

# Artifact: Decision log

A **single append-only TSV, one row per decision**, kept while an agent works unattended so a human who stepped away can audit what happened and decide whether to trust the result.

Six columns: `ts` (ISO8601), `phase`, `decision` (what was chosen, one line), `why` (the reason in plain words, *not* a jargon tag), `evidence` (a commit SHA, PR number, `file:line`, or an artifact, trace, or screenshot path — **never a paragraph**), and `result` (the outcome or predicate state: `tests green`, `reverted`, `pixel-diff 0`, `INCONCLUSIVE`, `open`).

```
ts	phase	decision	why	evidence	result
2026-05-24T09:40:00Z	harness	took screenshots of the old version before changing anything	so we can compare old against new and catch any visual change	scripts/snapshot.sh, baseline/	saved 120 reference screenshots
2026-05-24T11:15:00Z	widget	moved the widget styles over without changing how it looks	keep the change small and the result identical	commit 7c21e0a, pixel-diff 0	looks identical, tests pass
2026-05-24T12:30:00Z	widget	threw out a helper's work because its screenshots were blank	checked the real files instead of trusting its summary	worktree reset	reverted, tightened the instructions for next time
```

**Its distinguishing property among this wiki's artifacts is its reader.** [[artifact-handoff-doc]] and the state a [[store]] holds exist so the *next agent* can continue; a retrospective ([[artifact-retrospective]]) and a solution corpus ([[artifact-solution-doc]]) exist so *future work* starts ahead. A decision log exists so a **human who was not watching can reconstruct the reasoning after the fact** and locate the point where trust should stop. That is why evidence is a pointer rather than prose, why rows are single-line, and why the third example row above is a *reverted* decision — the log's value is concentrated in the moments the run went wrong.

Three rules govern it. **Append-only**: a wrong call gets a new row that supersedes it; history is never edited or deleted. **Decision points and checkpoints only** — a fork chosen, a unit completed with its verification result, a pivot or revert with its trigger, a blocker surfaced, a gate fixed — not every action. And **prefer evidence produced by committed scripts** over hand-made one-offs ([[pattern-tooling-leverage]]).

**Where it lives is a deliberate default.** It is a working artifact at `decisions.tsv` (or `.audit/<task-slug>.tsv` when several efforts run at once) and is left out of git, committed only when the work is ambitious enough that a reviewer needs the trail to trust the result. The trail is always kept; it becomes a repository artifact only when it has a reader.

## Produced by (backlinks)

pstack:

- [[pstack-show-me-your-work]] — owns the format, ships the `log.sh` helper, and defines the commit policy.
- [[pstack-figure-it-out]] — Phase D weaves a row in as each unit lands rather than saving the trail for the end.

## See Also
- [[artifact-handoff-doc]] — the agent-facing counterpart; that one is read by the next agent, this one by a human.
- [[artifact-retrospective]] — the after-the-fact synthesis; the decision log is the contemporaneous record.
- [[pattern-evidence-before-claims]] · [[pattern-tooling-leverage]] — the disciplines the evidence column enforces.
EOF

That is a direct rejection of the [[pattern-parallel-persona-review]] approach [[gstack]], [[bmad]], and [[addy-agent-skills]] take, and it makes pstack the wiki's purest [[pattern-cross-model-review]] instance. **The framework is multi-model by construction**, not as an option: [[pstack-setup-pstack]] exists solely to map roles to models, and [[pstack-how]], [[pstack-arena]], [[pstack-architect]], [[pstack-reflect]], and [[pstack-swarm]] each split work across model strengths. - **It refuses to plan, and says why.** *"why are there no planning skills? cursor already has a great plan mode which works great with pstack. but personally, i don't believe in planning. **the best spec is code.**"* There is no specify stage here at all and no spec artifact — the sharpest possible contrast with the spec-driven pole ([[speckit]], [[openspec]], [[nano-spec]], [[agent-os]]). What planning exists is [[pstack-figure-it-out]], reached only when **no** playbook fits, and [[pstack-architect]], which plans in *code shapes* (types, signatures, `not implemented` bodies) rather than in prose. This is the wiki's clearest instance of a framework putting its rigor entirely downstream of specification. - **A new pattern: [[pattern-candidate-grafting]].** [[pstack-arena]] fans out N attempts at the same artifact, picks a base, and then **harvests the losers** for the one or two ideas worth porting in. Everyone else's competing-candidates step discards the non-winners ([[gstack-design-shotgun]], [[mp-prototype]]); treating them as a parts bin is new here. - **A new pattern: [[pattern-tooling-leverage]].** *"Build the tool that does it or proves it… **the tool is the artifact a reviewer can rerun**."* The second clause is the contribution: the lever exists so a reviewer can re-derive the result, which is what makes it evidence rather than efficiency. - **A new pattern: [[pattern-idempotent-operations]].** Long-horizon agent work is interrupted constantly, so re-enterable steps are the precondition for [[pattern-autonomous-loop]] and [[pattern-session-handoff]] rather than an implementation nicety. - **A new artifact: [[artifact-decision-log]].** Every other durable artifact here is read by the *next agent* or by *future work*. [[pstack-show-me-your-work]]'s append-only TSV is read by **a human who was not watching**, so they can find the point where trust should stop. - **Suspension paged as its own procedure.** The mode skill carries a *Pause safely* playbook as the explicit complement of *Session pickup* — suspending in-flight work cleanly on an explicit pause, going offline, a restart, or imminent context compaction. Other frameworks page resumption ([[gstack-context-restore]], [[pstack-recall]]); pstack is the first to page the shutdown half. ## Signature mechanisms - **The sticky mode.** [[pstack-poteto-mode]] is `mode: true` with a `reminder` the harness re-injects every turn, so once entered it persists across turns and applies itself when a playbook matches or the task needs rigor. Every *other* skill in the plugin carries `disable-model-invocation: true`. The result is an inversion of [[superpowers]]' design, which makes every leaf auto-trigger — pstack makes the **router** persistent and every leaf explicitly manual, so there is exactly one thing deciding what fires. - **Playbooks copied in verbatim.** 23 playbook files, and the matched one's steps are copied into a todo list *verbatim* before any task-specific todos, with a skipped step staying in the list carrying a one-line `skip: `. Step text stays out of the router's context until needed, and skipping leaves a trace. - **The evidence ladder.** [[pstack-blast-radius]] grades every safety claim from *"you said so"* (worthless) through *pointed at the line*, *showed the bad case cannot happen*, *ran it*, up to *reproduced it in the running app* — and requires the writeup to **say where it stopped**, marking anything below rung 4 as **unproven**. The most operational form of [[pattern-evidence-before-claims]] in the wiki. - **The organizational-evidence sweep.** [[pstack-why]] discovers available MCP servers at run time and fans out one investigator per evidence category across source control, the issue tracker, long-form docs, team chat, infrastructure observability, error tracking, and the analytics warehouse, with shipped per-source playbooks and a rule that **a null result is a finding**. [[pstack-recall]] reuses the same machinery re-pointed at *current state*. No other framework here treats the organizational record as a first-class research corpus. - **Self-limiting rigor.** Several capabilities exist partly to say when *not* to apply themselves. [[pstack-tdd]] opens by listing when to skip the test and defines what a bad test is (*"prefer no new test over a bad test"*). [[pstack-how]] says *"when in doubt, take the simple path."* [[pstack-figure-it-out]] scales the evidence burden to blast radius. [[pstack-reflect]] skips trivial conversations because *"one-offs are not learnings."* This is [[pattern-scale-adaptive-planning]] applied to rigor rather than to ceremony. - **The comment-as-bug-report loop.** [[pstack-comment-sicko]] flags a comment on our own code as `MUST KILL` on the guilty *symbol*, and [[pstack-no-comments]] then implements the rename, extract, type, or reshape that makes the behavior obvious without prose — or, for a genuine constraint, **offers the cheapest type, runtime, test, or CI encoding and deletes the comment once it lands**. the framework's offer to be replaced as the entry point. - [[pstack-teach]] — explain a subsystem so a person understands it; diagram by diagram, no pedagogy theater. ### Cross-cutting — parallelism, prose, and setup (no single lifecycle stage) - [[pstack-poteto-mode]] — the sticky router; 23 playbooks and the inline principles index. - [[pstack-poteto-agent]] — the style-preserving subagent for any delegate inside a playbook step. - [[pstack-arena]] — N attempts at one artifact, pick a base, graft the losers. - [[pstack-swarm]] — N parallel cloud workers across slices or races, one aggregated report. - [[pstack-show-me-your-work]] — the append-only decision trail for unattended work. - [[pstack-unslop]] — cut AI tells; [[pstack-poteto-mode]] indexes them inline and reads the index at task start; a leaf is read in full only when applied. **Core** - [[pstack-principle-laziness-protocol]] — bias to deletion and the smallest change that solves the problem. - [[pstack-principle-foundational-thinking]] — get the data structures right so downstream code becomes obvious. - [[pstack-principle-redesign-from-first-principles]] — redesign as if the requirement had been foundational, not bolted on. - [[pstack-principle-attack-the-premise]] — when two fixes sharing a premise fail the same gate, question the premise. - [[pstack-principle-subtract-before-you-add]] — remove dead weight first, then build on the simpler base. - [[pstack-principle-minimize-reader-load]] — count layers and hidden state; collapse one-caller wrappers. - [[pstack-principle-outcome-oriented-execution]] — converge on the target architecture, no throwaway compatibility states. - [[pstack-principle-experience-first]] — user delight over implementation convenience; fewer polished features. - [[pstack-principle-exhaust-the-design-space]] — 2-3 competing prototypes compared side by side before committing. - [[pstack-principle-build-the-lever]] — build the tool that does or proves it; the tool is what a reviewer reruns. **Architecture** - [[pstack-principle-model-the-domain]] — encode the domain in a structure, not scattered conditionals. - [[pstack-principle-boundary-discipline]] — guards at system boundaries, pure business logic inside. - [[pstack-principle-type-system-discipline]] — make illegal states unrepresentable; parse at boundaries. - [[pstack-principle-make-operations-idempotent]] — converge to the same end state regardless of partial prior runs. - [[pstack-principle-migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis]] — migrate and delete in one wave. - [[pstack-principle-separate-before-serializing-shared-state]] — eliminate the sharing before serializing it. **Verification** - [[pstack-principle-prove-it-works]] — verify against the real artifact, not a proxy or "it compiles". - [[pstack-principle-fix-root-causes]] — trace each symptom to its root cause and fix it there. - [[pstack-principle-sequence-verifiable-units]] — units that each end in a check, ordered so the sequence proves itself. - [[pstack-principle-test-behavior-not-implementation]] — if it passes when every import returns `undefined`, rewrite or delete it. **Delegation** - [[pstack-principle-guard-the-context-window]] — route bulk to subagents, keep summaries in the main thread. - [[pstack-principle-never-block-on-the-human]] — proceed on reversible work; The other four layers all describe a *run*: the instructions it follows, the loop that executes them, where that loop runs, and the state it leaves behind. A `registry` describes what happens **before** the run — where the capabilities came from, who vouched for them, and what was allowed to be installed.

This is the layer that appears once capabilities stop being something you write and start being something you **acquire**. [[tessl]] states the premise plainly: *"Skills, rules, and docs are versioned, reviewed, and rolled out with the same rigor as code dependencies."* Discover, install, version, pin, roll back, scan, score, evaluate, deprecate — the full package-manager vocabulary, applied to agent context.

**Why it is a node and not a feature.** The wiki has been carrying this concern homeless for a long time. *Distribution* is a matrix dimension on both the [harness](harness/index.md) and [runtime](runtime/index.md) matrices; every `framework` page ends up with a free-text install line (*"`/plugin marketplace add EveryInc/compound-engineering-plugin`"*); and [[speckit]]'s page notes its packaging ecosystem is *"a distribution/customization layer no other framework here ships"* — an observation with nowhere to live. Minting the node gives those facts one home and converts the install lines into a stored `distributes:` edge.

**The boundary test — an independent product, not a vendor's shelf.** A marketplace shipped by a harness vendor for its own harness (Anthropic's plugin marketplace, `cursor/plugins`, opencode's community registry, Droid's plugin bundles) is a **harness feature**: it stays a row in the harness matrix and gets no node. A `registry` is a **separate product that distributes capabilities across harnesses it does not own**. The test is the same shape as the harness/runtime one: *page the thing you buy or deploy, not the feature your existing tool already has.* Without this rule the layer immediately sprawls to every vendor shelf, every MCP-server index, and every general agent marketplace.

**A corollary on artifact type.** This layer distributes **capabilities** — skills, rules, and the plugins that bundle them — as consumed by a *harness*. A registry of MCP servers (Smithery) distributes *tools*, which is an adjacent and genuinely different artifact; page one only if it also carries capabilities, and record the distinction rather than blurring it.

**What the layer is evidence *of*.** The wiki's core claim is that a `framework` is a bundle of `capability` pages. A registry makes the capability the independently versioned, independently installable unit — which is the framework bundle coming apart. [[bm-skills]] is a marketplace of unrelated utilities that had to be filed as a framework for want of anywhere better; [[superpowers]], [[addy-agent-skills]], [[compound-engineering]], and [[pstack]] all ship *through* a marketplace rather than as a tarball. Treat growth in this layer as the leading indicator that `framework` is becoming a distribution convenience rather than a methodology boundary, and re-read the framework pages against that when it does.

**Registry capabilities mostly implement no stage — with a caveat the store layer did not have.** As with a store, most of a registry's command surface is off-stage by construction: `tessl install` and `tessl plugin publish` perform no lifecycle step. Do **not** stretch a stage edge to make a registry look better covered. The caveat is that these products **grow sideways into the lifecycle** as they mature — Tessl ships `tessl code review` (agentic PR review), `tessl change risk`, and `tessl change verify`, which are genuine [[stage-review]] capabilities, plus `tessl launch` and `tessl schedule`, which spawn and schedule harnesses and are frankly *runtime-adjacent*. Wire the stage edge where the capability genuinely performs the stage, and record the runtime-adjacent surface as **prose**, per the harness/runtime boundary rule — do not mint a second node for one product's second act. When such a surface grows past prose, that is a re-ingest trigger, not a new node.

**The synthesis axis** — as with the other substrate layers, *collect instances then synthesize the dimensions they share*, but the dimensions are **supply concerns**: unit of distribution (skill \\| plugin \\| bundle) · public vs private index · versioning & rollback · provenance & signing · security scanning · quality scoring · impact measurement (evals) · policy & RBAC · audit trail · estate inventory · harness-agnosticism · open format vs proprietary · self-host vs SaaS. With one instance paged these live as a **comparison matrix** in `wiki/registry/index.md` and as prose per page — **not** minted as their own derived-node namespace. The same discipline parked for the runtime, harness, and store dimensions.

**Known instances, for the queue.** [[tessl]] is paged. Not yet ingested: **JFrog Agent Skills Registry** (the canonical package-registry incumbent entering the space; private, scanned and signed, claims the AgentSkills format and the OpenClaw registry protocol), **Google Cloud Skill Registry** (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform; private, hyperscaler-operated), **ClawHub** (community, vector search, `subtype: index`), **Agensi** (marketplace with a creator revenue split). An incumbent plus a hyperscaler plus an emerging open format is what distinguishes a category from a product, and is the evidence that justified minting the node on one paged instance. Also parked: **agentskills.io** and the AgentSkills format itself, which is a *standard* rather than a registry and probably belongs in `topic/` if it is captured at all.

**Ingesting a registry:** source → `raw/<registry>/YYYY-MM-DD-slug.md`; create `wiki/registry/<name>.md` with `type: registry`, a `subtype:`, `integrates_with:` → harness, `enables:` → pattern, and `distributes:` (usually `[]` at first); create one `capability` page per meaningful command family with `belongs_to:` → the registry (`implements:` usually `[]`, but wire it where a command genuinely performs a stage); create stub `pattern` pages for any new targets; add a **Supplied by (registry)** subsection to each enabled pattern; add an *Integrated by (registries)* bullet to each harness page's backlink roster and to the `harness/index.md` support matrix; refresh the matrix in `wiki/registry/index.md` and the `## registry` section in `catalogue.md`; log it. Re-derive stages only if a registry capability genuinely implements one.

"""
s = s[:i] + section + s[i:]
open('CONVENTIONS.md','w').write(s)
print("supply layer section inserted")

Company facts (funding, founding, the 2025 Framework pivot) from public reporting, recorded separately in the raw capture." raw: ["../../raw/tessl/2026-09-12-tessl-platform.md"] updated: 2026-09-12 --- # Tessl **Tessl** is *"an open platform for managing agentic development across your organization"* — the wiki's anchor instance of the [supply layer](index.md). Its premise is a single sentence, and the whole product follows from it: > **Context as code.** Skills, rules, and docs are versioned, reviewed, and rolled out with the same rigor as code dependencies. Founded in London in 2024 by **Guy Podjarny** (previously founder of Snyk), funded to $125M, advertising 3,000+ skills in its public registry. The company's own history is part of why it matters here: in 2025 it **paused its Framework product and removed Framework functionality from the rebuilt CLI to concentrate on the registry and agent integrations**. A company that set out to build a [framework](../catalogue.md#framework) and became a registry instead is direct evidence for this layer existing. ```mermaid flowchart LR AUTH["author
tessl skill new"] --> PKG["plugin
skills · rules · MCP · hooks"] PKG --> REV["review
is it well written?"] PKG --> SEC["security scan
is it safe?"] PKG --> EV["eval
does it work?"] REV --> PUB["registry
public or workspace"] SEC --> PUB EV --> PUB PUB --> POL{"install policy
+ RBAC"} POL --> AG["harness
Claude Code · Cursor · Codex · …"] INV["inventory
scan the org"] -.discovers.-> PUB ``` ## The six components | Component | What it is | |---|---| | **Registry & package manager** | Discover, install, version, and roll back skills and plugins like any other dependency. One searchable index of public and private context, agent-agnostic. | | **Governance** | Scan and score every skill against best practices and your own standards, with Snyk security scoring built in. RBAC over who can create, publish, and view; install and publish policies and required skills enforce standards across every workspace; full audit trail. | | **Evals** | Measure a skill's actual impact by running your agent on real tasks **with and without** the context. *"Every change ships with evidence instead of a guess."* | | **Observability** | See where skills actually **activate** across agent sessions, not just where they are installed. Mine agent logs for recurring mistakes. | | **Inventory** | Scan a GitHub org and map every skill across every repo in one living view. Surface duplicates and unmanaged copies — *"govern what you can see."* | | **Tessl Agent** | A conversational agent that drives the platform and autonomously monitors and improves the setup. Runs alongside your existing agents (open beta). | ## Distinctive contributions to the ontology - **It reproduces this wiki's [[stage-review]] ∥ [[stage-validate]] split, independently, for the skill corpus.** Tessl ships two quality instruments and is careful to distinguish them: a **review** checks a single skill against best practices (fast, cheap, automatic on publish, scored across validation / description / content) and a **scenario eval** runs an agent on real tasks with and without the context and compares the results. Its own summary is *"a review tells you whether a skill is **well written**; an eval tells you whether it **works**"* — which is the wiki's *is it good?* ∥ *does it work?* partition, arrived at from the supply side by a company that has never read this wiki. The strongest convergence evidence the layer produces. - **It closes an instrument the wiki had recorded as missing.** [[topic-ai-native-sdlc]] flagged continuous evals of the *agent's own configuration* as *"the one instrument nobody else ships"* — 20–50 real tasks re-run on any change to skills or hooks, with the pass rate enforced at merge. Tessl ships exactly that as [[tessl-eval]] plus [[tessl-scenario]], generating the scenarios, saving them **with the skill** as a regression suite, and gating CI on the score. The claim was not wrong — no *framework* ships it. It turns out to live in a different layer, which is the finding. - **It makes the `capability` the unit of trade.** A framework here is a bundle of capabilities; Tessl's unit is the **plugin** — a versioned bundle of skills, rules, MCP servers, and hooks, installed, versioned and updated as one, *"much like a package in npm or pip"* → [[artifact-capability-bundle]]. That is the framework bundle coming apart into independently versioned parts, and it is the trend this layer exists to track. - **A new threat surface: the capability supply chain.** [[pattern-supply-chain-scanning]] — scanning an installed skill for prompt injection buried in instructions, hardcoded secrets, suspicious download URLs, unverifiable external dependencies, and hidden or obfuscated text. Every guardrail pattern in the wiki so far bounds what the agent may **write** ([[pattern-edit-guardrails]]) or reach ([[gh-aw]]'s egress firewall). This one bounds what it may **read**, and it is the first time the wiki has paged instructions-as-attack-surface. - **A new measurement: [[pattern-capability-evals]].** Prove a capability changes behavior by A/B-ing the agent with and without it, against generated scenarios each pairing a task with a weighted rubric. *"That difference is the skill's value: proof it changes what the agent does, not just that it reads well."* ## Signature mechanisms - **Two kinds of context, loaded differently.** **Rules** apply *always* (team standards on every task); **skills** load *when relevant* (procedural workflows matched by description). A context-budget model stated as product architecture rather than as advice — [[pattern-context-engineering]] moved into the supply layer. - **The plugin carries more than context.** Alongside skills and rules a plugin can ship **MCP servers** (live tools) and **hooks** that run deterministic commands on `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SessionStart`, and `Stop`. So a registry install can extend the *harness*, not just the prompt — the supply layer reaching down into harness primitives. - **Three nouns that are easy to confuse, kept apart.** A **plugin** is content and capability; a **workspace** is ownership (the team boundary that decides who may publish and see private plugins, and where the inventory lives); a **project** is location (the stable anchor tying Tessl to one repository so eval results stay attached to the right codebase as branches come and go). - **Security warns, it does not block.** Findings are severity-graded and critical/high are surfaced at install, *"warning rather than blocking and leaving the decision to you."* A deliberate, recorded choice: policy blocks (that is what install policies are for), scanning informs. Contrast [[gh-aw]], whose threat verdict hard-blocks every safe-output job. - **A forkable rubric.** The default review rubric scores general best practices; an organization **forks it** to encode its own bar and applies it to every review — *"much like static analysis for code."* Standards as a versioned artifact rather than a document ([[artifact-standards]]). - **Inventory before governance.** *"Govern what you can see."* [[tessl-inventory]] scans GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket and indexes every skill and config it finds across every repo, surfacing duplicates and unmanaged copies. The layer's answer to the problem that a team's real skill estate is unknown before anyone tries to manage it. - **Harness-agnostic by construction.** `tessl init` detects and auto-configures **Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, GitHub Copilot CLI, and GitHub Copilot for VS Code**; anything else that speaks MCP is configured manually, with shipped recipes for **OpenCode** and **OpenClaw**. The integration is an MCP server (`tessl mcp start`) plus written config, so the same skill works everywhere. *"Write context once; Tessl distributes it everywhere."* - **Open, with an exit.** *"Tessl builds on open standards and writes your skills, rules, and config as plain artifacts in your repo, so you own your agent setup and can walk away with it at any time."* Worth recording because the lock-in question is the obvious objection to a commercial layer sitting upstream of everything else. ## Capabilities by function ### The package manager ([[artifact-capability-bundle]]) - [[tessl-install]] — install, uninstall, list, outdated, update; from the registry, a filesystem path, a GitHub repo, or a specific commit; per-repo or global. - [[tessl-search]] — search the registry and install from the results. - [[tessl-init]] — initialize a repo and **auto-configure every detected coding agent**; `tessl project` anchors results to the repository. ### Authoring and publishing - [[tessl-skill]] — scaffold, import, lint, publish, and unpublish a single skill. - [[tessl-plugin]] — create, lint, migrate, pack, inspect, publish, unpublish, and archive the versioned bundle. ### Quality, safety, and measurement - [[tessl-review]] — score a skill's structure, description, and content against a rubric; *is it well written?* - [[tessl-review-security]] — the Snyk-powered scan for prompt injection, secrets, suspicious URLs, and hidden text ([[pattern-supply-chain-scanning]]). - [[tessl-review-fix]] — iteratively improve a skill until it clears a score threshold. - [[tessl-scenario]] — generate the task scenarios an eval grades against, server-side feasibility-checked → [[artifact-eval-suite]]. - [[tessl-eval]] — run the agent with and without the context and score the difference; *does it work?* ([[pattern-capability-evals]]). ### Governance and estate - [[tessl-workspace]] — workspaces, organizations, roles, members, and API keys: the ownership and RBAC boundary. - [[tessl-inventory]] — scan a source-control org and index every skill and config across every repo. - [[tessl-environment]] — named environments carrying secrets and MCP-server wiring into a run. ### Lifecycle capabilities (the sideways growth) - [[tessl-code-review]] — agentic PR review with configurable **lenses**, as a GitHub App or a CLI ([[stage-review]]). - [[tessl-change-risk]] — assess a diff's risk and exit non-zero when human review is required ([[stage-review]]). - [[tessl-change-verify]] — run configured LLM-judge **verifiers** over changed files with caching, sampling, and CI annotations ([[stage-review]]). ### Execution surface (runtime-adjacent — see the boundary note below) - [[tessl-launch]] — launch a coding agent, or run an installed skill locally or **in the cloud** against a repo. - [[tessl-schedule]] — cron schedules that run a registry plugin against a repo on an interval, with pause, resume, and manual trigger. - [[tessl-agent]] — the conversational platform agent, with its own MCP server management. - [[tessl-mcp]] — `mcp start` (the integration every harness connects to) and `mcp proxy` (a workspace MCP gateway). ## The layer boundary, honestly Tessl is not *only* a registry, and the wiki should say so rather than tidy it away. [[tessl-launch]] spawns harnesses including cloud runs, and [[tessl-schedule]] puts them on a cron — which is, by the [execution layer](../runtime/index.md)'s own definition, runtime behavior. Tessl's own tagline points straight at it: *"It takes you from scaling skills to **building your software factory**"* (see [[topic-software-factory]]). It is filed as a `registry` under the [harness/runtime boundary rule](../CONVENTIONS.md#the-harness-layer) applied one layer over: **page the product's center of gravity, record the second act as prose.** The centre of gravity is unambiguous — the docs, the CLI's bulk, the funding thesis, and the pivot away from Framework all point at governing the supply of capabilities. # Registry

*The supply layer — the versioned index capabilities are discovered in, vouched for, and installed from, before any run begins.*

The wiki's other four layers all describe a **run**: a [framework](../catalogue.md#framework) is the instructions it follows, a [harness](../harness/index.md) is the loop that executes them, a [runtime](../runtime/index.md) decides where that loop runs, and a [store](../store/index.md) is the state it leaves behind. A **registry** describes what happened *before* the run — where the capabilities came from, who scanned and scored them, and what policy allowed to be installed.

This layer appears at the moment capabilities stop being something you write and become something you **acquire**. [[tessl]] states the premise directly:

> **Context as code.** Skills, rules, and docs are versioned, reviewed, and rolled out with the same rigor as code dependencies.

A registry performs no [SDLC stage](../sdlc-stage/index.md) as a layer, and connects to the ontology through `integrates_with:` → harness, `enables:` → pattern, and `distributes:` → framework \| capability, plus the `belongs_to:` backlinks from its own command surface. The full schema is in [CONVENTIONS](../CONVENTIONS.md#the-supply-layer-registries).

## Members

| Registry | Subtype | What it is | Surface | Updated |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [[tessl]] | `platform` | *"An open platform for managing agentic development across your organization."* Registry and package manager, governance (RBAC, install/publish policy, Snyk scanning), evals, observability, org inventory, and a platform agent. Founded by Snyk's Guy Podjarny; pivoted away from its own framework product to build this. | 101 commands · 20 pages | 2026-09-12 |

One instance paged. The node was minted on one because the **category** is unambiguous even where the wiki's coverage is not — see the queue below.

## The queue

| Instance | Shape | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **JFrog Agent Skills Registry** | `platform`, private-first | The canonical package-registry incumbent entering the space: scanned, signed, approved skills served from a private registry, claiming the **AgentSkills** format and the **OpenClaw registry protocol**. An incumbent arriving is the strongest category signal available. |
| **Google Cloud Skill Registry** | `platform`, private | A hyperscaler shipping a private, low-latency skill repository inside the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. |
| **ClawHub** | `index` | Community registry with vector search over skills and gateway plugins — the discovery-only pole, and the evidence that made `index` a subtype rather than an edge case. |
| **Agensi** | `index` | Marketplace for `SKILL.md` skills and MCP servers with curation, security scanning, and a creator revenue split. The commercial-marketplace shape. |

Parked deliberately: **agentskills.io** and the AgentSkills format itself are a *standard*, not a registry, and belong in `topic/` if captured at all. **Smithery** is a registry of **MCP servers** — tools rather than capabilities — which is the adjacent-artifact case the [conventions](../CONVENTIONS.md#the-supply-layer-registries) tell you to record rather than blur.

## The boundary test

**An independent product, not a vendor's shelf.** A marketplace shipped by a harness vendor for its own harness — Anthropic's plugin marketplace, `cursor/plugins`, opencode's community registry, Droid's plugin bundles — is a **harness feature**. It stays a row in the [harness matrix](../harness/index.md) and gets no node. A `registry` is a separate product distributing capabilities across harnesses it does not own.

Two consequences worth stating, because both are live cases in this wiki:

- **[[pstack]] ships through `cursor/plugins`, and that does not make `cursor/plugins` a registry.** It is Cursor's shelf for Cursor. The install route stays prose on the framework page.
- **[[bm-skills]] stays a `framework`, and the tension is real.** It is a Claude Code plugin *marketplace* of unrelated utilities whose own page says it is *"deliberately not a full-SDLC framework"* — so it reads like a registry. But it fails the test in both directions: it is single-harness, and it is a GitHub repo of three skills rather than a product that distributes anyone else's work. It is best understood as a **framework whose bundle is unusually loose**, which is the thing the framework node already strains to cover. Re-file it only if it starts carrying third-party skills.

## The synthesis axis

With one member paged, the shared dimensions live here as prose rather than a matrix — the same discipline parked for the [runtime](../runtime/index.md), [harness](../harness/index.md), and [store](../store/index.md) dimensions. The dimensions to fill in as instances arrive:

**unit of distribution** (skill \| plugin \| bundle) · **index visibility** (public \| private \| both) · **versioning & rollback** · **provenance & signing** · **security scanning** · **quality scoring** · **impact measurement (evals)** · **policy & RBAC** · **audit trail** · **estate inventory** · **harness-agnosticism** · **open format vs proprietary** · **self-host vs SaaS**

Public-vs-private is a dimension here and not a subtype, because the platforms are generally both at once: Tessl runs a public registry and private per-team workspaces off the same index. The subtype axis is how much of the supply chain the product owns — a searchable `index` versus a governed `platform`.

## What one instance already shows

**The layer reproduces the review ∥ validate split, independently.** Tessl ships a **review** (is the skill well written? — fast, structural, automatic on publish) and a **scenario eval** (does it work? — run the agent with and without it, score the difference) and is explicit that they answer different questions. That is [[stage-review]] ∥ [[stage-validate]] arrived at from the supply side, by a company with no knowledge of this wiki. Convergence of that kind is the main thing the wiki produces, and finding it in a new layer on the first ingest is a good sign the layer is real.

**Instructions are now an attack surface.** [[pattern-supply-chain-scanning]] is the layer's genuinely new pattern: scanning a capability for prompt injection buried in its text, hardcoded secrets, suspicious download URLs, and hidden or obfuscated content. Every guardrail pattern already here bounds what the agent may *write* ([[pattern-edit-guardrails]]) or *reach* ([[gh-aw]]'s egress firewall). This bounds what it may *read*. Installing a skill from a public index is running someone else's prompt with your agent's permissions, and this is the layer that noticed.

**The framework is coming apart.** The wiki's core claim is that a framework is a bundle of capabilities. A registry makes the capability the independently versioned, installable unit, and four paged frameworks ([[superpowers]], [[addy-agent-skills]], [[compound-engineering]], [[pstack]]) already ship *through* a marketplace rather than as a download. Treat growth in this layer as the leading indicator that `framework` is becoming a distribution convenience rather than a methodology boundary.

**The layer leans toward the factory.** Tessl already ships agent launching, cloud runs, and cron schedules, and says out loud that it takes you *"from scaling skills to building your software factory"*. A supply platform that can also run what it distributes is one product decision away from being a [runtime](../runtime/index.md). Watch the boundary; see the [honest note](tessl.md#the-layer-boundary-honestly) on the Tessl page.

# Pattern: Capability evals (prove the instructions changed the behavior)

Measure whether a **capability actually works** by running an agent on real tasks twice — once without it and once with it — and scoring the difference. Keep the tasks as a suite alongside the capability so every later change re-runs them.

> An evaluation runs an agent on real tasks twice, once without the skill and once with it, then scores the difference. That difference is the skill's value: **proof it changes what the agent does, not just that it reads well.** — [[tessl]]

The A/B is the whole point and is what separates this from ordinary review. A skill can be well-structured, well-described, and clearly written and still change nothing about the output; without a baseline run you cannot tell. The unit under test is not the code the agent wrote, it is **the instructions that shaped it**.

## Why it is distinctive

Every other verification pattern here tests the **product**: [[pattern-test-driven-development]] tests the code, [[pattern-evidence-before-claims]] tests the claim about the code, [[pattern-deterministic-gates]] runs a program over the code. This one tests **the agent's own configuration** — the layer that decides how all of those get done. It is the QA gate rebuilt for the thing that now varies.

That makes it the first pattern in the wiki whose subject is a `capability` page rather than a piece of software, and it is why it belongs to the [supply layer](../registry/index.md): once capabilities are traded as versioned dependencies, "does this dependency help?" becomes a question someone has to answer with evidence rather than taste.

**The scenarios become a regression suite.** *"The scenarios are saved with the skill, so anyone who changes it later can re-run the same scenarios and confirm it still behaves as expected."* This is the mechanism that makes a shared skill corpus safe to edit — the failure mode it addresses is a team that will not touch a skill because nobody can tell what a change would break → [[artifact-eval-suite]].

**It has a cheap sibling it should not be confused with.** Tessl runs both, and names the distinction: a **review** is fast, structural, and automatic on publish (*is it well written?*); an **eval** is slow, task-based, and deliberate (*does it work?*). Reach for the eval before publishing something others will use in agents you never see.

## Supplied by (registry)

- [[tessl]] — [[tessl-eval]] runs the A/B and scores it; [[tessl-scenario]] generates the tasks, each server-side feasibility-checked so the suite exercises the skill rather than padding it, each pairing a task with a weighted rubric. Evals attach to a project (a repository anchor), so results stay tied to the right codebase.

- [[pstack-reflect]] — gates its own accepted learnings with a structural-enforcement check, which is the same question (does this instruction earn its place?) answered by judgment rather than by an A/B.

# Pattern: Supply-chain scanning (the instructions are an attack surface)

Scan a capability **before it is installed** for content designed to subvert the agent that loads it: prompt injection buried in the instructions, hardcoded secrets, suspicious download URLs, unverifiable external dependencies, and hidden or obfuscated text. Grade findings by severity and surface them at install time.

## Why it is distinctive

The wiki already has guardrail patterns, and this one is pointed the other way. [[pattern-edit-guardrails]] bounds what the agent may **write** — confirm destructive commands, lock edits to a directory, route writes through validated jobs. [[gh-aw]]'s firewall bounds what it may **reach**. This bounds what it may **read**.

That gap existed because capabilities used to be things you wrote. Once they are things you **install from a public index**, the threat model changes completely: *"installing skills from public sources exposes you to new supply-chain and prompt-injection risk"* ([[tessl]]). A skill is a prompt that runs with your agent's permissions, so an untrusted skill is untrusted code — and unlike code, it is plain prose that reads as innocuous and is not compiled, sandboxed, or diffed by anyone.

**It is the classic software supply chain, one level up.** Everything the industry learned about dependency confusion, typosquatting, and malicious transitive packages applies to a registry of skills, which is why the instance that anchors it is built by [[tessl]] (founded by Snyk's founder, with Snyk scoring built in) and why the other serious entrant is JFrog. The failure mode is familiar and the artifact is new.

**Warning is a real design choice, not a weakness.** Tessl surfaces critical and high findings at install, *"warning rather than blocking and leaving the decision to you"*, and keeps hard enforcement in a separate mechanism — install policies, which are governance rather than scanning. Contrast [[gh-aw]], whose threat-detection verdict hard-blocks every safe-output job. Both are defensible; the split matters because a scanner that blocks gets disabled, and a policy that warns gets ignored.

**Hidden text is the tell worth remembering.** Of the listed detections, *hidden and obfuscated text* is the one with no analogue in ordinary dependency scanning. It exists because the consumer is a language model reading prose, so an attack can hide in whitespace, comments, or encoding that no human reviewer would notice and no linter would flag.

## Supplied by (registry)

- [[tessl]] — [[tessl-review-security]] runs the scan and can gate CI on severity; findings are graded and surfaced on install, and a serious finding on a third-party skill *"can signal a supply-chain attack, so treat it with care"*. [[tessl-inventory]] is the precondition at org scale: you cannot scan an estate you have not indexed.

## See Also
- [[pattern-edit-guardrails]] — bounds what the agent may write; this bounds what it may read. The pair covers both directions.
- [[pattern-deterministic-gates]] — where a scan becomes enforcement (a CI gate failing on high or critical).

- [[artifact-capability-bundle]] — the unit being scanned.
- [[topic-ai-native-sdlc]] — managed settings with marketplace pinning, the enterprise control that sits alongside scanning.

# Artifact: Capability bundle

A **versioned package of agent context and extensions, installed and updated as one unit** — the unit of trade in the [supply layer](../registry/index.md). [[tessl]] calls it a *plugin*, and the comparison it reaches for is the right one: *"Everything in a plugin is installed, versioned, and updated as one unit, much like a package in npm or pip."*

What it carries is broader than instructions:

- **Skills** — procedural workflows loaded when the task matches ([[artifact-skill-doc]]).
- **Rules** — standards applied to every task, always on.
- **MCP servers** — live tools and data, not just text.
- **Hooks** — deterministic commands bound to agent lifecycle events (`PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SessionStart`, `Stop`).
- **Evals** — the scenarios it is graded against, kept with the thing they grade ([[artifact-eval-suite]]).

That composition is the interesting part. A bundle is not only *context*; through hooks and MCP servers it extends the **harness itself**, so installing one from a registry changes the agent's execution primitives and not just its prompt. The supply layer reaches down into the harness layer at exactly this point.

**Why it is a separate artifact from [[artifact-skill-doc]].** A `SKILL.md` is one piece of process knowledge. A bundle is a *release*: it has a version, a changelog, an owner, a visibility setting, a security score, an eval suite, and a rollback path. The wiki already records frameworks shipping through marketplaces ([[superpowers]], [[addy-agent-skills]], [[compound-engineering]], [[pstack]]); this is the shape they ship *as*, and paging it separately is what lets the layer say that the framework bundle is coming apart into independently versioned parts.

# Artifact: Eval suite

A directory of **scenarios that grade a capability**, versioned alongside the capability itself. Each scenario pairs a **task** an agent is asked to perform with a **rubric of weighted criteria** used to score the result. Running the suite means running the task twice — once with the capability loaded and once without — and comparing ([[pattern-capability-evals]]).

In [[tessl]] it lives at `evals/` inside the bundle, one scenario per subdirectory, and can be generated or hand-written. Generated scenarios pass a server-side **feasibility check** before being saved, *"so the generator gives you tests that actually exercise the skill rather than filler"* — a quality gate on the tests themselves, which is unusual and worth recording.

**Its function is to make a shared skill corpus editable.** The failure mode it addresses is stated plainly by the product it comes from: *"You can't tell whether a skill actually improves agent output, so no one risks changing it."* Once the suite exists, *"anyone who changes it later can re-run the same scenarios and confirm it still behaves as expected"* — the same role a regression test plays for code, for a thing that is not code.

**It is a regression suite for prose**, which is what makes it new. Every other test artifact in this wiki grades the software the agent produced. This one grades the instructions that produced it, and it is the durable half of the instrument [[topic-ai-native-sdlc]] recorded as shipped by nobody: 20–50 real tasks re-run whenever the configuration changes, with the score enforced at merge.

## Produced by (backlinks)

Tessl:

- [[tessl-scenario]] — generates scenarios from a plugin, from two commits, or from real PRs; feasibility-checks them server-side; downloads them into the bundle's `evals/`.
- [[tessl-eval]] — runs the suite, scores the with/without difference, and can lint the scenarios themselves.
